issues.item: Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
issues.explanation: 'Being in nature similar to where it happened' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of life-threatening illness, which typically involves medical/health contexts rather than a natural-environment trauma setting.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: 'Avoid grief reminders' implies bereavement/loss of another person, which does not fit the stated trauma type of life-threatening illness unless there is an unreported death-related trauma; it is not supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: 'Fear of rage' is weakly connected to the rest of the profile: the other appraisals and memory items center on damage, unreality, and role failure after illness, not anger-based dyscontrol. This makes the appraisal set less internally coherent.

vignette:
Mei-Ling Chen was forty-two, a project manager who had built her career on precision and control, when a routine physical revealed a cancerous tumor in her colon. The surgery that followed was successful by any medical measure, but the weeks in the intensive care unit had carved something into her that the oncologist's discharge summary never mentioned. She still remembered the moment she woke from anesthesia: the cold of the room seeping through the thin blanket, the sharp, sweet smell of antiseptic cleaner, and the sight of a saline drip needle taped to the back of her hand. That single instant-temperature, odor, equipment-became a kind of trapdoor in her mind.

In the months afterward, the trapdoor would spring open without warning. A chill wind on her walk to the office would bring the memory flooding back not as a coherent story, but as a raw, wordless terror: her heart racing, her skin flushed with heat, yet the actual images of the hospital were blurred or missing, leaving only the emotion. Other times the reverse happened-certain moments from the ICU were excruciatingly clear, like the doctor's face as he checked the drain tube, while the days before and after were completely blank. After each such vivid intrusion, she found herself noticing medical imagery everywhere - the white of a delivery van, the beep of a crosswalk signal - things that had never bothered her before. The memory felt so extreme that Mei-Ling often thought, this can't have really happened to me. Yet her body kept insisting it had.

She started to manage the intrusions as best she could. Whenever she caught a whiff of something clinical-hand sanitizer in a colleague's cubicle, the sterile wipes in the break room-she would deliberately push the whole event out of her mind, trying to erase it. She also began to monitor her own thoughts throughout the day, scanning for any hint of the trauma, because she was terrified that letting even one fragment surface meant she was losing her grip on reality. That thought-monitoring, she had come to believe, was the only thing keeping her from going crazy. But it also made her hyperaware of every trace of a trigger: the cold metal of her desk lamp, the sight of a paperclip that resembled an IV port. If she saw a first-aid kit in a colleague's bag, she would physically look away and recite her schedule to block the image. She avoided hospitals entirely, canceling follow-ups and rescheduling her annual physical until the reminders stopped coming. At work, she started taking the stairs instead of the elevator, because the elevator's antiseptic-cleaned walls smelled like the ICU.

These strategies seemed necessary, but they came with a cost. The more she tried to erase the memory, the more fragmented it became-emotion without image, clarity without context-and the more unreal the whole experience felt. And the more she scanned for signs of madness, the more convinced she grew that her life had been destroyed by what happened. She had always defined herself through her roles: competent project manager, dependable wife, the one who held everything together. Now she saw herself as someone who had failed in her most important role-taking care of her own body. The trauma had permanently damaged her, she believed, and no amount of planning could fix that. This conviction that she was irreparably broken kept dragging her back to the memory of the ICU, as if replaying it might reveal when the damage had actually begun.

The loop tightened over a year. A sudden drop in temperature in an air-conditioned conference room would flash her back to the ICU's cold, and she would excuse herself to stand in the hallway, trying to push the memory away. The emotional surge, without any clear image, only reinforced her belief that her body was broken and her mind was unraveling. Once, when her husband Mark turned on the car's air conditioning in January, she recoiled and snapped at him-a minute response that left them both shaken. She began checking the weather each morning to avoid any chance of cold air. The avoidance itself became a trigger: even the thought of a hospital made her mind spiral, and she would start monitoring her thoughts again to prevent the spiral from taking hold.

What finally brought Mei-Ling to a therapist's office was not the panic itself, but the moment she realized she was now afraid of her own refrigerator. The cold blast when she opened the freezer had sent her gasping across the kitchen, and Mark had found her crouched on the tile floor, trying to recite project deadlines aloud to block the memory. She told him she needed help. In the session, she sat rigidly, her hands clasped, and said she was most afraid that nothing could undo the damage-that her life had been permanently taken from her, and she was only waiting for the next trigger to prove it.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that the patient's negative appraisals (e.g., feeling that the trauma has permanently damaged her or that her mind is unraveling) directly influence or drive the intrusive memory.
No paragraph conveys that the intrusive memory itself leads to new triggers or increases sensitivity to existing triggers; the vignette shows triggers activating memory but not the reverse.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that the patient's negative appraisals (e.g., feeling that the trauma has permanently damaged her or that her mind is unraveling) directly influence or drive the intrusive memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the intrusive memory itself leads to new triggers or increases sensitivity to existing triggers; the vignette shows triggers activating memory but not the reverse.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
